body:
What is described looks less like a chores problem than an agreement problem. Three details do most of the work: agreements are reached but later mean different things to different people; schedules keep changing; one flatmate has stopped attending the conversation.

On the first: when people agree and then dispute what was agreed, the usual cause is not bad faith but underspecification. "I'll do the kitchen" feels complete in the moment but leaves the contentious parts — when, how often, what counts as done — to be filled in privately by each person, differently. So my first conjecture is that the flat is paying the cost of tacit agreements, and that making them cheaply explicit (written, visible, each with a one-line definition of done) shrinks most of the dispute surface without any fairness negotiation at all.

On the second: changing schedules mean any fixed rota will keep failing, and each failure becomes fresh material for argument. A system keyed to the week's actual availability — tasks claimed against real shifts rather than persons bound to fixed days — fits the flat's actual constraint.

On the third I am least certain. Avoidance is data about the conversation: it has presumably become aversive or felt-pointless. But it could equally be overload, conflict-aversion, disengagement, or someone quietly doing less and dodging accountability. The remedy differs in each case, so the first move worth making is a low-stakes one-to-one with that friend about the process — what makes these talks something to avoid — before proposing anything to the group.

The course I'd sketch: that private conversation first; then a short, explicitly provisional trial — a shared task list where every task carries its definition of done and is claimed against the coming week's shifts, with a pre-agreed no-blame rule for misses (the task gets re-claimed rather than litigated) and a fixed date two weeks out to revise it. The two-week framing matters: it lowers the stakes enough for the avoider to re-enter, and it treats the system as revisable rather than a verdict.

A stance note: goodwill is the resource actually being spent here. While schedules are unstable, some weekly unevenness is worth absorbing deliberately rather than litigating; the one option I'd rule out is silent score-keeping. And a caveat: I cannot tell from this description who does more, or whether a fairness fight sits underneath the chore talk — if it does, parts of this account need revising, so it should be held as conjecture, not diagnosis.

surfaces which possible cause of avoidance is operative.","depends":["c3"]},{"id":"cm2","type":"commitment","text":"Adopt an explicitly provisional, availability-keyed, written task system instead of a permanent rota.","action":"Propose a two-week trial: a shared visible task list where each task carries a one-line definition of done and is claimed against the coming week's actual shifts, with a set date to revise it.","consequence":"Shrinks the ambiguity surface, matches allocation to real availability, and lowers the stakes enough for the avoider to re-enter.","depends":["c1","c2"]},{"id":"cm3","type":"commitment","text":"Pre-agree a no-blame miss rule as part of the trial.","action":"Agree in advance that a missed task is re-claimed or swapped at the next check-in rather than litigated as a fault.","consequence":"Keeps failures logistical rather than moral, which is what makes the system survivable under schedule churn.","depends":["cm2"]},{"id":"cm4","type":"commitment","text":"Treat goodwill as the protected resource: tolerate temporary unevenness while schedules are unstable, refuse silent score-keeping, and raise fairness openly if that is the real issue.","action":"Absorb some week-to-week unevenness deliberately and voice fairness concerns explicitly rather than keeping a private ledger.","consequence":"Protects the friendship, which is what the recurring arguments are actually spending."},{"id":"p1","type":"problem","text":"Unknown why the friend avoids the conversations — overload, conflict-aversion, disengagement, or quietly doing less and dodging accountability; if the avoider is actually disengaged or benefiting from doing less, a process-first approach postpones the fairness confrontation and may entrench the pattern.","bearing":"If true, cm1 delays the harder conversation and the cm2 trial may be gamed; the objection's own force depends on facts not yet available."}],"uptake":["c1","c2","c3","cm1","cm2","cm3","cm4","p1","p2"]}
